title: Miketz: the Hanukkah portion
hookLine: Miketz almost always falls during Hanukkah: dreams and lights in the dark season

cards: Early winter, north of the equator. Dark by five. Cold car in the morning, dark driveway at night.
And in window after window, small flames in a row, one more every night. That's Hanukkah.
Hanukkah has fixed dates on the Jewish calendar, and the weekly Torah reading moves through the year in order, so the two keep meeting.
The Shabbat of Hanukkah almost always reads Miketz, the portion of Pharaoh's dreams and Joseph's rise.

teach.b: First, the holiday. Hanukkah means dedication. In the time the books of the Maccabees describe, a Greek-Syrian king banned Jewish practice and set up an idol in the Temple in Jerusalem.

A small band led by the Maccabee family rebelled, won, and rededicated the Temple. The Talmud adds the story of the oil: they found only one small jar of pure oil, enough for one day, and it burned for eight.

teach.h: ONE JAR OF OIL, EIGHT NIGHTS.
teach.b: So Jews light for eight nights, adding one light each night, as the school of Hillel taught, and set the lights where people outside can see them. Now the portion.
Miketz is full of dreams: Pharaoh's cows and grain, and Joseph, who once dreamed as a boy, now reading dreams for a king.

teach.h: DREAMS AND A PLAN FOR LEAN YEARS.
teach.b: Seven fat years, seven lean, and a plan to get through the dark ones. Some readers hear a match: both are about light in a dark time.
Hanukkah begins near the end of a Hebrew month, when the moon is thin, close to the longest nights of the year in the northern half of the world.
And Joseph's story is a light in the dark too: the prisoner forgotten for two years ends up feeding the hungry from Egypt's stores.
On the Shabbat of Hanukkah, the reading from the prophets is from Zechariah, who sees a golden lampstand in a vision.

teach.h: NOT BY MIGHT, NOR BY POWER.
teach.b: In the old Jewish Publication Society translation: "Not by might, nor by power, but by My spirit, saith the LORD of hosts."
Dreams in the dark, lights in the dark. Neither pretends the night is short. Each puts one small light in it.

how: Jews light the Hanukkah menorah for eight nights, adding one light each night, often in a window, with blessings; on the Shabbat of Hanukkah, synagogues read Miketz and the prophetic reading from Zechariah's vision of the lampstand.

games.q: you've found one small jar of pure oil, enough for one day, and you need eight. what do you do?
games.why: the Talmud says they lit it anyway, and it burned for eight days. that's why Hanukkah lasts eight nights.

practice: If you have a candle and it's safe, light it now; if not, picture one, a single small flame.

Watch the light, and remember a dream you once had for your life, not a night dream but a hope, maybe one that got put away in a dark year. Hold it near the flame for a while; you don't have to decide anything, just let it be seen.
